thesis.title: Normative Incorporation
thesis.thesis: A genuine social fact is a coincidental regularity that has been incorporated into a public practice of justification, exception, and change, so that its persistence is explained by normative integration rather than by causal continuity.
thesis.argument_sketch: Many regularities begin accidentally, but they become institutional when people cite them as norms, justify deviations, and coordinate their future behavior around them. The difference is not that the pattern is more stable, but that it has become a public reason. For example, a habitual salute becomes a convention when it can be excused, challenged, and revised. Mere regularities lack this incorporation. They are explained by causal continuity rather than by normative integration.
thesis.why_new: It offers a developmental diagnostic that explains how a regularity can cross the boundary into a social fact, which is underemphasized in static metaphysical accounts.

objection.objection: The central contrast fails because the public practices of justification, exception, and change are already causally stable social practices; using them to explain how a mere regularity becomes a social fact both presupposes the social status it needs to explain and collapses the supposed non-causal normative explanation back into causal continuity.
objection.rationale: If unanswered, the thesis either collapses into the causal-regularity view it rejects or invokes an unexplained noncausal normative force. Public citation, excuse, challenge, and revision persist only through stable dispositions, such as beliefs, expectations, sanctions, authority, and communicative routines, so normative integration is part of the causal explanation of persistence, not an alternative to it (Searle, The Construction of Social Reality, 1995; Rawls, 'Two Concepts of Rules', 1955; Lewis, Convention, 1969). The account also cannot identify a mere regularity as incorporated into a public practice without already presupposing social facts about what counts as public justification, legitimate exception, and authorized change; hence it cannot non-circularly explain how accidental regularities become genuine social facts.

closest_work.work: H. L. A. Hart, The Concept of Law (1961; 3rd ed. 2012), especially ch. 2, 'Social Rules', and the account of secondary rules (rules of recognition, change, adjudication)
closest_work.relation: Closest. Hart already argues that a mere regularity becomes a social or legal rule when it is treated as a standard, deviations are criticized or justified, and the practice has public criteria for recognition, change, and adjudication; this supplies the 'regularity plus public justification/exception/change' and normative-persistence parts of the thesis, though as a theory of social and legal rules rather than a general theory of all social facts.

closest_work.work: David Lewis, Conventions: A Philosophical Study (1969), especially the treatment of conventional regularities and their arbitrary or contingent origins
closest_work.relation: Related but not sufficient. Lewis anticipates that a convention can have an accidental origin and that its stability is explained by common expectations, salience, and equilibrium, not by causal continuity; this covers the 'coincidental regularity' half, but not the public practice of justification, exception, and change.

novelty.note: The exact formulation as a general account of 'genuine social facts' does not appear to be a standard published thesis in those exact terms. The core argument is substantially Hartian: the move from regularity to rule or institution is made public and normative by criticism, justification, and public criteria for change. The accidental-origin point is close to Lewis, but Lewisian conventions are explained by mutual expectations rather than public normative justification. For novelty, the author would need to distinguish the claim from Hart's internal point of view and secondary rules, from Lewisian coordination equilibria, and from Searle's institutional facts, and show why 'public reason' or 'normative integration' adds something not already captured by these accounts.

# From Coincidence to Public Reason: Normative Integration and the Explanation of Social Facts

## 1. Introduction

Much social ontology begins with the claim that social facts are facts about groups, institutions, conventions, or collective intentions. That broad starting point is right, but it can obscure a more precise distinction: between regularities that merely occur in social settings and regularities that have been made into public reasons. I want to defend the following thesis.

> A genuine social fact is a coincidental regularity that has been incorporated into a public practice of justification, exception, and change, so that its persistence is explained by normative integration rather than by causal continuity.

By “coincidental regularity” I do not mean a random accident in the metaphysical sense. I mean a pattern that, prior to or absent normative incorporation, is not treated by its participants as a reason-bearing item. It may be stable, habitual, environmentally produced, or coordinated. Its persistence, if any, is explained by prior causes, dispositions, or background regularities. What it lacks is the public grammar in which it can be cited as a norm, excused as an exception, or revised by public act. A genuine social fact, in the strong sense, is not merely a stable pattern. It is a pattern that has become a public reason.

The paper has four parts. First, I describe coincidental regularities and their explanatory profile. Second, I specify the three operations—justification, exception, and change—by which a regularity is normatively integrated. Third, I explain why normative integration, not causal continuity, explains the persistence of the resulting social fact. Fourth, I answer the strongest objection: that the public practices required for normative integration are themselves causally stable social practices, so the account is circular and collapses normative explanation into causal explanation.

## 2. Coincidental Regularities

A useful starting point is Hume’s observation that many institutions arise out of custom and convention (Hume 1987). Lewis offers an influential account of conventions as regularities sustained by mutual knowledge and coordination (Lewis 1969). Both emphasize the centrality of regularity. But regularity alone does not explain the distinctive status of social facts.

Let R be a pattern of behavior, event, or representation in a population. R is a mere coincidental regularity, relative to a context C, if three conditions obtain. First, R’s continuation is not explained by participants citing R as a norm or public reason. Second, deviations from R are not publicly represented as violations, excusable failures, or authorized exceptions. Third, changes in R are not treated as amendments, suspensions, or public revisions. R may persist because of habits, environmental regularities, causal chains, or simple coordination, but it is not yet a public reason.

Consider a community in which people always nod to one another. The nodding may be very stable. It may be caused by shared upbringing, a local greeting style, or the social costs of ignoring others. But suppose no one can justify the nod as a norm: “I nod because that is what we do here” is only a historical report, not an appeal to a public standard. If someone fails to nod, no one expects an excuse; no one says the greeting was suspended; no one revises the form of the greeting by public decision. The pattern is social in a thin sense—people are social beings—but it is not a genuine social fact in the strong sense. It is explained by causal continuity, not by normative integration.

I am not claiming that every social fact has a prehistory as a pure accident. I am claiming that, prior to incorporation, the pattern is best described non-normatively: as a coincidence of prior causes rather than as a public reason. The important point is that the missing feature is not empirical stability. A causal chain can be extremely stable. What is missing is a public grammar of normative accountability. A mere regularity does not generate obligations, excuses, or authorized changes. It can stop without anyone having failed. It can continue without anyone having justified it. It can vary without anyone having amended anything. These features distinguish it from a genuine social fact.

## 3. Normative Integration

A regularity becomes a genuine social fact when it is incorporated into a public practice P that does three things.

The first operation is justification. P allows R to be cited as a public reason. “We meet on Tuesdays” is not merely a report that past meetings occurred; it is an appeal to a shared standard. Participants can invoke R to explain their own actions and to challenge others. If someone misses the meeting, the question “Why were you not there?” can be answered by reference to the meeting itself, or to a public exception. The practice is public because it is answerable: participants can ask for reasons, appeal to the practice, and be held accountable for failing to engage with it. This matches Raz’s idea that norms are public reasons that can be invoked and challenged (Raz 1975). It also fits Searle’s account of institutional facts as status functions: something counts as something else within a shared context (Searle 1995). A habitual salute, for example, becomes a convention when the salute can be excused, challenged, and revised, not merely when it is a repeated gesture.

The second operation is exception. P represents deviations from R in a public vocabulary that distinguishes violations, excusable failures, and authorized exceptions. If the Tuesday meeting is missed, the absence may be a breach requiring apology, an excused absence due to illness, or an authorized suspension. The existence of this grammar is decisive. Bicchieri emphasizes the role of mutual expectations and reactive attitudes in social norms (Bicchieri 1998), but the key feature here is not merely that people react to deviations, but that the deviations are classified in a public way. A mere regularity has no such classification. A failure to repeat a regularity is just a failure; it is not a violation, because there was no norm to violate.

The third operation is change. P authorizes revision, suspension, or amendment of R. The Tuesday meeting can be moved to Thursdays by public decision. The greeting can be replaced by a handshake. A rule can be repealed. Hart’s account of legal systems is useful here: a legal system is not a mere aggregate of primary rules; it includes secondary rules that provide criteria for recognition, change, and adjudication (Hart 1961). The analog for social facts is this: a genuine social fact is not just a behavior that persists; it is a pattern embedded in a practice that can say how it may be altered. A mere regularity can cease, but it cannot be amended in the normative sense.

These three operations require publicness. I do not mean only that the pattern is visible. I mean that participants are jointly committed to maintaining a practice of justification, exception, and change. Gilbert’s notion of joint commitment captures the idea that participants are collectively bound and can demand participation (Gilbert 1996). Bratman’s account of shared intention adds that such practices involve mutual obligations and expectations (Bratman 2014). The point is not that every participant must constantly endorse R. It is that the practice is publicly available: it can be cited, challenged, excused, and revised without each token requiring a private intention.

The result of normative integration is not that R is more stable. It is that R has become a term in a public practice. It is now a public reason. The difference is explanatory: the pattern’s persistence is no longer explained only by its causal history, but by its place in a practice of public justification, exception, and change.

## 4. Explaining Persistence

I need to be precise about the claim that a social fact’s persistence is explained by normative integration rather than by causal continuity. The claim is not anti-causal. Norms are realized in the world. They are sustained by beliefs, expectations, sanctions, institutions, habits, and other causal processes. Elster is right to stress that norms have social and causal lives (Elster 1989). But the explanation of a social fact’s persistence is not simply the causal continuity of prior instances.

Consider the Tuesday meeting again. Before incorporation, if no meeting occurs, the explanation is a causal story: the storm canceled it, the organizer forgot, the bus was late. After incorporation, the same physical absence may be explained differently. It may be a violation requiring repair, an excused absence, or an authorized suspension. The meeting persists not because past meetings causally generate future meetings, but because participants treat the meeting as a public commitment and because the practice supplies public reasons for maintaining, repairing, or revising it.

Normative integration also explains identity over time. A social fact can persist through changes in tokens, participants, and behavior. A law may persist after its original enactors are dead. A property may persist through transfer. A company may persist after all shares change hands. A meeting may be postponed and reconvened. Causal continuity of the original pattern is not necessary for the persistence of the social fact. What matters is that the public practice treats the later instances, suspensions, and revisions as continuations, exceptions, or authorized changes of the same fact. Causal continuity alone cannot explain this. A mere regularity that breaks is just gone; a social fact can survive a break because the public practice recognizes the break as an exception or an authorized alteration.

Thus “rather than causal continuity” means the following. Causal continuity may be a necessary background for any physical persistence. But it is not the explanation of social persistence. The explanation is that the pattern has been made into a public reason. It is now a fact whose continuation, failure, and change are evaluated within a public grammar of norms. That is the explanatory contrast.

## 5. The Referee’s Objection

The strongest objection to this account is that the central contrast fails. The objection goes as follows: the public practices of justification, exception, and change are already causally stable social practices. To explain how a mere regularity becomes a social fact by appeal to such a practice both presupposes the social status it needs to explain and collapses the supposed non-causal normative explanation back into causal continuity.

This objection is important, and I take it seriously. I will answer it in three parts. First, the presupposition is local, not vicious. Second, causal stability is not the explanatory variable. Third, the objection, if taken to its full strength, would eliminate a distinction that is conceptually and empirically real.

### 5.1 The Presupposition Is Local, Not Vicious

We should not expect an explanation of a particular social fact to be derived from non-social materials. The thesis is not that sociality as such emerges from non-social regularities. It is that a particular pattern acquires the status of a genuine social fact by being incorporated into a broader normative practice. The background practice may itself be a social fact. That is not circular.

To explain why a particular token is an English sentence, we appeal to English, a social practice. The practice is not the token. To explain why a particular parcel is private property, we appeal to a legal practice. The legal practice is social, but the property fact is not identical with the entire legal practice. To explain why a particular gesture is a salute, we appeal to the practice of saluting. The practice may itself be an institutional social fact, but the gesture’s being a salute is explained by its place in that practice, not by the practice’s existence simpliciter.

The status to be explained here is not “sociality” in general. It is the fact that this regularity is a public reason. The public practice of justification, exception, and change supplies the form under which a regularity can be social. The regularity is not already included in that form; it is incorporated into it. The explanation is vicious only if we explained the public practice itself by the very regularity whose social status is at issue. But the account does not do that. It explains a derivative social fact by its incorporation into a broader normative context.

This local character is common in social ontology. A promise is explained by the practice of promising. A legal obligation is explained by the legal system. A currency is explained by monetary institutions. There need be no first social fact. Social facts are relational and often hierarchical. The argument does not require a foundation of non-social facts. It requires only that, within an already public normative context, a pattern can be distinguished from a genuine social fact by the presence or absence of a public grammar of justification, exception, and change.

### 5.2 Causal Stability Is Not the Explanatory Variable

The second part of the objection says that, because the public practice is causally stable, the normative explanation collapses into causal continuity. This confuses causal realization with explanatory type.

Norms are causally realized. A promise is sustained by memory, trust, expectations, sanctions, and dispositions. A legal rule is sustained by courts, education, institutional habits, and social pressure. A convention is sustained by coordination, habit, and reputation. None of this is mysterious. But the explanation of a promise’s being an obligation is not “the causal process is stable.” It is that the utterance has been made into a public commitment that can be cited, challenged, excused, and revised. The explanation of a legal obligation is not “the legal system is causally stable.” It is that the obligation is generated by a rule within a public system of recognition, change, and adjudication. The causal stability of the system is a condition of its persistence, but it is not the explanation of the normative status of particular facts within it.

The relevant contrast is between two explanatory claims. Call them (C) and (N). (C) says: R persists because earlier Rs and their causes produced later Rs. (N) says: R persists because it is incorporated into a public practice that treats R as a reason and supplies public procedures for exception and change. A mere regularity can be explained by (C) alone. A genuine social fact can also have a causal history, but its persistence as a social fact is explained by (N). Both (C) and (N) may be true of the same physical pattern after incorporation, but they are different explanations. Noting that norms have causal conditions does not reduce (N) to (C).

An analogy may help. A chess move is caused by the previous move, the player’s intentions, and the physical state of the board. But the move’s being a legal move is explained by the rules, not by causal continuity. The rules are socially maintained; that does not make the rule-explanation merely causal. The rules are the explanatory variable. Their causal stability is not.

A second clarification is needed. “Causal continuity” has two senses. In the minimal sense, any persistence requires causal connection. The thesis does not deny this. In the stronger sense, the persistence of a pattern is fully explained by its prior causal history. Normative integration rejects this stronger sense. A social fact can persist through causal breaks. A law may be suspended and revived. A meeting may be postponed and reconvened. A property may be transferred. A company may survive a complete change of shareholders. Its identity as the same fact is maintained by the public practice, not by an unbroken causal chain. The public practice’s causal stability is not identical with the fact’s social continuity.

The objection also assumes that if a public practice is causally stable, then any regularity incorporated into it is explained by that stability. But that would make the explanatory variable too broad. If causal stability were enough, any stable causal process in a social setting would count as a social fact. Yet a stable habit, a stable pattern of aggressive behavior, and a stable natural regularity can all be causally continuous. What distinguishes a genuine social fact is not causal stability but public normative integration: the pattern can be cited as a reason, deviations can be classified as exceptions or violations, and changes can be authorized as revisions. The causal stability of the surrounding practice is a background condition, not the explanatory contrast.

### 5.3 Why the Objection Is Too Strong

If the objection were correct, the distinction between mere regularities and social facts would collapse. But the distinction is conceptually real and empirically important. A stable habit may be caused by prior behavior, but it does not require excuses, generate violations, or permit public amendment. A stable convention may solve a coordination problem, but its normative force depends on its being citable as a public reason, not merely on its being a regularity. A stable legal rule may be widely ignored, but it remains a legal fact because the public practice of justification, exception, and change still recognizes it.

The public practice is social, yes. But the regularity’s social status is explained by its incorporation into that practice, not by the practice’s causal stability. The practice supplies a normative space: a space in which patterns can be justified, excused, and changed. Once a regularity occupies that space, its persistence is explained by its normative role. The causal stability of the practice is part of the story of how the practice endures, but it is not the story of how the regularity becomes a public reason.

This response preserves the original thesis without making it anti-causal. Normative integration is not a fourth force alongside physical causation. It is a way in which causal processes are organized around public reasons. The explanation is normative because it appeals to the participants’ public grammar of justification, exception, and change. It is not merely causal because the explanatory variable is the pattern’s role as a public reason, not the mere continuity of prior instances.

## 6. Conclusion

The contrast at the center of this paper is not between social facts and everything else, but between regularities that are explained by causal continuity and regularities that have been incorporated into a public practice of justification, exception, and change. A genuine social fact is a pattern that has become a public reason. Its persistence is explained not by the length or stability of a causal chain, but by the fact that participants treat it as a norm, can justify their adherence to it, can classify deviations as exceptions or violations, and can revise it by public acts.

The strongest objection asks whether the public practice required for this account is not itself a social fact, and whether the account therefore presupposes what it explains or collapses normative explanation into causal explanation. The answer is that the account is local, not foundational: it explains a particular pattern’s social-fact status by its incorporation into a broader normative context. And the answer is that causal realization is not explanatory collapse: the causal stability of the public practice is a background condition, while the explanatory variable is the pattern’s place in a public grammar of norms. Social facts are not more stable regularities. They are regularities that have been made public, answerable, and revisable.

# From Coincidence to Public Reason: Normative Integration and the Explanation of Social Facts

## 1. Introduction

Much social ontology begins with the claim that social facts are facts about groups, institutions, conventions, or collective intentions. That broad starting point is right, but it can obscure a more precise distinction: between regularities that merely occur in social settings and regularities that have been made into public reasons. I want to defend the following thesis.

> A genuine social fact is a coincidental regularity that has been incorporated into a public practice of justification, exception, and change, so that its persistence is explained by normative integration rather than by causal continuity.

By “coincidental regularity” I do not mean a random accident in the metaphysical sense. I mean a pattern that, prior to or absent normative incorporation, is not treated by its participants as a reason-bearing item. It may be stable, habitual, environmentally produced, or coordinated. Its persistence, if any, is explained by prior causes, dispositions, or background regularities. What it lacks is the public grammar in which it can be cited as a norm, excused as an exception, or revised by public act. A genuine social fact, in the strong sense, is not merely a stable pattern. It is a pattern that has become a public reason.

The paper has four parts. First, I describe coincidental regularities and their explanatory profile. Second, I specify the three operations—justification, exception, and change—by which a regularity is normatively integrated. Third, I explain why normative integration, not causal continuity, explains the persistence of the resulting social fact. Fourth, I answer the strongest objection: that the public practices required for normative integration are themselves causally stable social practices, so the account is circular and collapses normative explanation into causal explanation.

## 2. Coincidental Regularities

A useful starting point is Hume’s observation that many institutions arise out of custom and convention (Hume 1987). Lewis offers an influential account of conventions as regularities sustained by mutual knowledge and coordination (Lewis 1969). Both emphasize the centrality of regularity. But regularity alone does not explain the distinctive status of social facts.

Let R be a pattern of behavior, event, or representation in a population. R is a mere coincidental regularity, relative to a context C, if three conditions obtain. First, R’s continuation is not explained by participants citing R as a norm or public reason. Second, deviations from R are not publicly represented as violations, excusable failures, or authorized exceptions. Third, changes in R are not treated as amendments, suspensions, or public revisions. R may persist because of habits, environmental regularities, causal chains, or simple coordination, but it is not yet a public reason.

Consider a community in which people always nod to one another. The nodding may be very stable. It may be caused by shared upbringing, a local greeting style, or the social costs of ignoring others. But suppose no one can justify the nod as a norm: “I nod because that is what we do here” is only a historical report, not an appeal to a public standard. If someone fails to nod, no one expects an excuse; no one says the greeting was suspended; no one revises the form of the greeting by public decision. The pattern is social in a thin sense—people are social beings—but it is not a genuine social fact in the strong sense. It is explained by causal continuity, not by normative integration.

I am not claiming that every social fact has a prehistory as a pure accident. I am claiming that, prior to incorporation, the pattern is best described non-normatively: as a coincidence of prior causes rather than as a public reason. The important point is that the missing feature is not empirical stability. A causal chain can be extremely stable. What is missing is a public grammar of normative accountability. A mere regularity does not generate obligations, excuses, or authorized changes. It can stop without anyone having failed. It can continue without anyone having justified it. It can vary without anyone having amended anything. These features distinguish it from a genuine social fact.

## 3. Normative Integration

A regularity becomes a genuine social fact when it is incorporated into a public practice P that does three things.

The first operation is justification. P allows R to be cited as a public reason. “We meet on Tuesdays” is not merely a report that past meetings occurred; it is an appeal to a shared standard. Participants can invoke R to explain their own actions and to challenge others. If someone misses the meeting, the question “Why were you not there?” can be answered by reference to the meeting itself, or to a public exception. The practice is public because it is answerable: participants can ask for reasons, appeal to the practice, and be held accountable for failing to engage with it. This matches Raz’s idea that norms are public reasons that can be invoked and challenged (Raz 1975). It also fits Searle’s account of institutional facts as status functions: something counts as something else within a shared context (Searle 1995). A habitual salute, for example, becomes a convention when the salute can be excused, challenged, and revised, not merely when it is a repeated gesture.

The second operation is exception. P represents deviations from R in a public vocabulary that distinguishes violations, excusable failures, and authorized exceptions. If the Tuesday meeting is missed, the absence may be a breach requiring apology, an excused absence due to illness, or an authorized suspension. The existence of this grammar is decisive. Bicchieri emphasizes the role of mutual expectations and reactive attitudes in social norms (Bicchieri 1998), but the key feature here is not merely that people react to deviations, but that the deviations are classified in a public way. A mere regularity has no such classification. A failure to repeat a regularity is just a failure; it is not a violation, because there was no norm to violate.

The third operation is change. P authorizes revision, suspension, or amendment of R. The Tuesday meeting can be moved to Thursdays by public decision. The greeting can be replaced by a handshake. A rule can be repealed. Hart’s account of legal systems is useful here: a legal system is not a mere aggregate of primary rules; it includes secondary rules that provide criteria for recognition, change, and adjudication (Hart 1961). The analog for social facts is this: a genuine social fact is not just a behavior that persists; it is a pattern embedded in a practice that can say how it may be altered. A mere regularity can cease, but it cannot be amended in the normative sense.

These three operations require publicness. I do not mean only that the pattern is visible. I mean that participants are jointly committed to maintaining a practice of justification, exception, and change. Gilbert’s notion of joint commitment captures the idea that participants are collectively bound and can demand participation (Gilbert 1996). Bratman’s account of shared intention adds that such practices involve mutual obligations and expectations (Bratman 2014). The point is not that every participant must constantly endorse R. It is that the practice is publicly available: it can be cited, challenged, excused, and revised without each token requiring a private intention.

The result of normative integration is not that R is more stable. It is that R has become a term in a public practice. It is now a public reason. The difference is explanatory: the pattern’s persistence is no longer explained only by its causal history, but by its place in a practice of public justification, exception, and change.

## 4. Explaining Persistence

I need to be precise about the claim that a social fact’s persistence is explained by normative integration rather than by causal continuity. The claim is not anti-causal. Norms are realized in the world. They are sustained by beliefs, expectations, sanctions, institutions, habits, and other causal processes. Elster is right to stress that norms have social and causal lives (Elster 1989). But the explanation of a social fact’s persistence is not simply the causal continuity of prior instances.

Consider the Tuesday meeting again. Before incorporation, if no meeting occurs, the explanation is a causal story: the storm canceled it, the organizer forgot, the bus was late. After incorporation, the same physical absence may be explained differently. It may be a violation requiring repair, an excused absence, or an authorized suspension. The meeting persists not because past meetings causally generate future meetings, but because participants treat the meeting as a public commitment and because the practice supplies public reasons for maintaining, repairing, or revising it.

Normative integration also explains identity over time. A social fact can persist through changes in tokens, participants, and behavior. A law may persist after its original enactors are dead. A property may persist through transfer. A company may persist after all shares change hands. A meeting may be postponed and reconvened. Causal continuity of the original pattern is not necessary for the persistence of the social fact. What matters is that the public practice treats the later instances, suspensions, and revisions as continuations, exceptions, or authorized changes of the same fact. Causal continuity alone cannot explain this. A mere regularity that breaks is just gone; a social fact can survive a break because the public practice recognizes the break as an exception or an authorized alteration.

Thus “rather than causal continuity” means the following. Causal continuity may be a necessary background for any physical persistence. But it is not the explanation of social persistence. The explanation is that the pattern has been made into a public reason. It is now a fact whose continuation, failure, and change are evaluated within a public grammar of norms. That is the explanatory contrast.

## 5. The Referee’s Objection

The strongest objection to this account is that the central contrast fails. The objection goes as follows: the public practices of justification, exception, and change are already causally stable social practices. To explain how a mere regularity becomes a social fact by appeal to such a practice both presupposes the social status it needs to explain and collapses the supposed non-causal normative explanation back into causal continuity.

This objection is important, and I take it seriously. I will answer it in three parts. First, the presupposition is local, not vicious. Second, causal stability is not the explanatory variable. Third, the objection, if taken to its full strength, would eliminate a distinction that is conceptually and empirically real.

### 5.1 The Presupposition Is Local, Not Vicious

We should not expect an explanation of a particular social fact to be derived from non-social materials. The thesis is not that sociality as such emerges from non-social regularities. It is that a particular pattern acquires the status of a genuine social fact by being incorporated into a broader normative practice. The background practice may itself be a social fact. That is not circular.

To explain why a particular token is an English sentence, we appeal to English, a social practice. The practice is not the token. To explain why a particular parcel is private property, we appeal to a legal practice. The legal practice is social, but the property fact is not identical with the entire legal practice. To explain why a particular gesture is a salute, we appeal to the practice of saluting. The practice may itself be an institutional social fact, but the gesture’s being a salute is explained by its place in that practice, not by the practice’s existence simpliciter.

The status to be explained here is not “sociality” in general. It is the fact that this regularity is a public reason. The public practice of justification, exception, and change supplies the form under which a regularity can be social. The regularity is not already included in that form; it is incorporated into it. The explanation is vicious only if we explained the public practice itself by the very regularity whose social status is at issue. But the account does not do that. It explains a derivative social fact by its incorporation into a broader normative context.

This local character is common in social ontology. A promise is explained by the practice of promising. A legal obligation is explained by the legal system. A currency is explained by monetary institutions. There need be no first social fact. Social facts are relational and often hierarchical. The argument does not require a foundation of non-social facts. It requires only that, within an already public normative context, a pattern can be distinguished from a genuine social fact by the presence or absence of a public grammar of justification, exception, and change.

### 5.2 Causal Stability Is Not the Explanatory Variable

The second part of the objection says that, because the public practice is causally stable, the normative explanation collapses into causal continuity. This confuses causal realization with explanatory type.

Norms are causally realized. A promise is sustained by memory, trust, expectations, sanctions, and dispositions. A legal rule is sustained by courts, education, institutional habits, and social pressure. A convention is sustained by coordination, habit, and reputation. None of this is mysterious. But the explanation of a promise’s being an obligation is not “the causal process is stable.” It is that the utterance has been made into a public commitment that can be cited, challenged, excused, and revised. The explanation of a legal obligation is not “the legal system is causally stable.” It is that the obligation is generated by a rule within a public system of recognition, change, and adjudication. The causal stability of the system is a condition of its persistence, but it is not the explanation of the normative status of particular facts within it.

The relevant contrast is between two explanatory claims. Call them (C) and (N). (C) says: R persists because earlier Rs and their causes produced later Rs. (N) says: R persists because it is incorporated into a public practice that treats R as a reason and supplies public procedures for exception and change. A mere regularity can be explained by (C) alone. A genuine social fact can also have a causal history, but its persistence as a social fact is explained by (N). Both (C) and (N) may be true of the same physical pattern after incorporation, but they are different explanations. Noting that norms have causal conditions does not reduce (N) to (C).

An analogy may help. A chess move is caused by the previous move, the player’s intentions, and the physical state of the board. But the move’s being a legal move is explained by the rules, not by causal continuity. The rules are socially maintained; that does not make the rule-explanation merely causal. The rules are the explanatory variable. Their causal stability is not.

A second clarification is needed. “Causal continuity” has two senses. In the minimal sense, any persistence requires causal connection. The thesis does not deny this. In the stronger sense, the persistence of a pattern is fully explained by its prior causal history. Normative integration rejects this stronger sense. A social fact can persist through causal breaks. A law may be suspended and revived. A meeting may be postponed and reconvened. A property may be transferred. A company may survive a complete change of shareholders. Its identity as the same fact is maintained by the public practice, not by an unbroken causal chain. The public practice’s causal stability is not identical with the fact’s social continuity.

The objection also assumes that if a public practice is causally stable, then any regularity incorporated into it is explained by that stability. But that would make the explanatory variable too broad. If causal stability were enough, any stable causal process in a social setting would count as a social fact. Yet a stable habit, a stable pattern of aggressive behavior, and a stable natural regularity can all be causally continuous. What distinguishes a genuine social fact is not causal stability but public normative integration: the pattern can be cited as a reason, deviations can be classified as exceptions or violations, and changes can be authorized as revisions. The causal stability of the surrounding practice is a background condition, not the explanatory contrast.

### 5.3 Why the Objection Is Too Strong

If the objection were correct, the distinction between mere regularities and social facts would collapse. But the distinction is conceptually real and empirically important. A stable habit may be caused by prior behavior, but it does not require excuses, generate violations, or permit public amendment. A stable convention may solve a coordination problem, but its normative force depends on its being citable as a public reason, not merely on its being a regularity. A stable legal rule may be widely ignored, but it remains a legal fact because the public practice of justification, exception, and change still recognizes it.

The public practice is social, yes. But the regularity’s social status is explained by its incorporation into that practice, not by the practice’s causal stability. The practice supplies a normative space: a space in which patterns can be justified, excused, and changed. Once a regularity occupies that space, its persistence is explained by its normative role. The causal stability of the practice is part of the story of how the practice endures, but it is not the story of how the regularity becomes a public reason.

This response preserves the original thesis without making it anti-causal. Normative integration is not a fourth force alongside physical causation. It is a way in which causal processes are organized around public reasons. The explanation is normative because it appeals to the participants’ public grammar of justification, exception, and change. It is not merely causal because the explanatory variable is the pattern’s role as a public reason, not the mere continuity of prior instances.

## 6. Conclusion

The contrast at the center of this paper is not between social facts and everything else, but between regularities that are explained by causal continuity and regularities that have been incorporated into a public practice of justification, exception, and change. A genuine social fact is a pattern that has become a public reason. Its persistence is explained not by the length or stability of a causal chain, but by the fact that participants treat it as a norm, can justify their adherence to it, can classify deviations as exceptions or violations, and can revise it by public acts.

The strongest objection asks whether the public practice required for this account is not itself a social fact, and whether the account therefore presupposes what it explains or collapses normative explanation into causal explanation. The answer is that the account is local, not foundational: it explains a particular pattern’s social-fact status by its incorporation into a broader normative context. And the answer is that causal realization is not explanatory collapse: the causal stability of the public practice is a background condition, while the explanatory variable is the pattern’s place in a public grammar of norms. Social facts are not more stable regularities. They are regularities that have been made public, answerable, and revisable.
